cell-free extracts of the obligate intracellular bacterium Rickettsia prowazekii, the agent of epidemic typhus, contain demonstrable activities of enzymes involved in glutamate catabolic and tricar-boxylic acid cycle pathways but do not have detectable activities of enzymes of glycolysis.

the enzymology of R. typhii.

the characterization of the enzymatic activity of Rickettsiae and the elucidation of the metabolic pathway(s) of these organisms.

Rickettsia is a parasite which has retained the capacity to utilize the citric acid cycle, but has lost the ability to synthesize ATP by oxidative phosphorylation, and has lost the ability of catabolizing glucose to pyruvate by glycolysis, and has lost its capacity to synthesize ATP from pyruvate and ADP by the Embden-Meyerhof pathway.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the rickettsial tricarboxylate and glutamate pathways are operative in the cell, and that the glycolytic pathway is not.

rickettsiae have the enzymatic potential to synthesize energy-rich phosphates by oxidative catabolism but not by glycolysis, and thus are dependent for their energy needs on the oxidative catabolisms of their host cells.
the Rickettsia is a highly specialized organism, which has lost many metabolic capabilities, including glycolysis, but has retained the capacity for catabolism through the tricarobxylic acid cycle.
The main takeaway from our work is that
R. typhi is a metabolically active organism that can be studied with cell-free extracts.
R. typhi is a facultative intracellular parasite that has a limited capacity for catabolism and that the host cell may be required for its growth and maintenance.

R. typhi, unlike C. burnetii, does not appear to be able to synthesize ATP through the glycolysis pathway, but instead, like most obligate intracellular bacteria, must depend on the host for its energy.
